PoSME: Proof of Sequential Memory Execution
via Latency-Bound Pointer Chasing
with Causal Hash Binding

David Condrey
ORCID: 0009-0003-1849-2963 Affiliation: WritersLogic Inc.
San Diego, California
david@writerslogic.com
Abstract

We introduce PoSME (Proof of Sequential Memory Execution), a cryptographic primitive that enforces sustained sequential computation via latency-bound pointer chasing over a mutable arena. Each step reads data-dependent addresses, writes a block whose value and causal hash are mutually dependent (symbiotic binding), and chains the result into a global transcript. This yields three properties: (1) Ω⁡(K)\Omega(K) sequential memory-step enforcement, (2) high TMTO resistance (10×10{\times} at write density ρ=4\rho{=}4, with a formal S⋅T=Ω⁡(K2)S\cdot T=\Omega(K^{2}) space-time lower bound), and (3) a tight ASIC advantage bound by DRAM random-access latency rather than bandwidth. Benchmarks across 17 CPU platforms and 4 GPU architectures demonstrate that hash computation is under 3.5% of step cost and GPU hardware is 14–19×\times slower than a consumer CPU. PoSME requires no trusted setup and provides a foundation for verifiable delay, authorship attestation, and Sybil resistance.

I Introduction

Many systems require proof that a party performed sustained, sequential computation under concrete resource constraints [18, 29, 28]: ASIC-resistant mining, authorship attestation, Sybil resistance, and verifiable delay. Existing primitives each capture only part of this objective.

VDFs [1] certify sequential time but are insensitive to memory; a VDF ASIC gains arbitrary speedup via faster ALUs. PoSW [2] proves graph traversal but over static, immutable memory. Memory-hard functions such as Argon2id [3] raise per-evaluation cost via memory pressure, but are single-shot primitives with no chain proof system. Composing them (e.g., chaining Argon2id with Merkle sampling) yields independent properties that do not reinforce each other. Table I summarizes the gap.

PoSME fills this gap. Mutability is essential: in a static arena with independent blocks, any block can be recomputed from the seed in O⁡(1)O(1), so the adversary need not store the arena at all. A mutable arena forces storage because block values evolve unpredictably under the ROM during execution. The persistent mutable arena is the computation state. Each step reads dd blocks at addresses determined by the previous read’s hash output (pointer chasing), modifies the arena in-place, and chains a causal hash through the written block. Data and causal hash are symbiotically bound: neither can be fabricated without the other. The bottleneck is DRAM random-access latency (40–50 ns on DDR5), with hash computation (∼3{\sim}3 ns) under 3% of cost. HBM3 is only 1.3×\times faster than DDR5 at random access; GPU hardware is 14–19×\times slower than CPUs at this workload.

Main Contributions.

  • •

    Novel Construction: We define PoSME, the first primitive combining mutable arena state, data-dependent pointer-chase addressing, and symbiotic causal hash binding, formalized over a Boolean hypercube to enable binary-field folding.

  • •

    Space-Time Security: We prove a formal S⋅T=Ω⁡(K2)S\cdot T=\Omega(K^{2}) lower bound for dynamic causal DAGs (Theorems 3–4), extended to adaptive adversaries (Theorem 5) with no factor loss.

  • •

    ROM Validation: We validate the ROM-uniformity assumption mathematically (Theorem 6) and empirically at the full recommended scale (N=224N{=}2^{24}, 5.4×1085.4{\times}10^{8} reads, χ2/df=1.0004\chi^{2}/\text{df}=1.0004).

  • •

    Hardware Validation: We validate ASIC resistance across 17 CPU and 4 GPU platforms, showing GPUs are 14–19×\times slower and GPU throughput is choked by VRAM capacity.

  • •

    IVC Design: We provide a concrete Binius arithmetization (144,512 Boolean constraints per step) with analyzed fold cost and pipelining feasibility.

Section II presents the construction, including the hypercube formulation and IVC design. Section III provides the security analysis (Theorems 1–6). Section IV gives the empirical validation. Section VII discusses limitations.

I-A Related Work

PoSW. Cohen and Pietrzak [2] prove traversal of a depth-robust graph via Fiat-Shamir [22] sampled Merkle proofs. PoSME differs by introducing a mutable arena (not a static DAG), where the access pattern is data-dependent rather than fixed, and each node carries a causal hash binding its value to its write history.

MHFs. scrypt [8], proven maximally memory-hard by [31], introduced memory-hardness; Argon2id [3] achieves bandwidth-hardness with ∼2×{\sim}2{\times} single-pass TMTO penalty and 88–16×16{\times} ASIC advantage [4]. RandomX [21] targets CPU-egalitarianism via random code execution, achieving 22–5×5{\times} ASIC bound. PoSME achieves higher TMTO resistance (10×10{\times} at ρ=4\rho{=}4) and a tighter ∼2×{\sim}2{\times} ASIC bound via latency-hardness rather than bandwidth- or compute-hardness.

PoS/PoST. Proofs of Space [9] and Space-Time [2] enforce storage over static graphs. PoSME extends to a mutable arena with per-block temporal binding. CMC. Alwen et al. [5] formalized cumulative memory complexity for static pebbling. PoSME’s causal DAG is dynamic, requiring the new framework of §III-D.

II Construction

II-A Design Intuition

Before presenting the formal algorithms, we outline the three core design principles that differentiate PoSME from existing sequential primitives:

  1. 1.

    Data-Dependent Pointer Chasing: The address of each subsequent read depends on the value of the current read. This enforces a strict sequential chain that cannot be parallelized.11 1 The hardness of parallelizing pointer chasing has a long history in communication complexity; Nisan and Wigderson [20] initiated this line; Viola [13] gives a recent tight Ω⁡(n/k+k)\Omega(n/k+k) bound for kk-step pointer chasing.

  2. 2.

    Mutable Arena State: Unlike static graph-based proofs, the arena evolves at every step. Recomputing an evicted block requires replaying its write chain (O⁡(ρ)O(\rho) hashes per miss; Theorem 2).

  3. 3.

    Symbiotic Causal Binding: Every write binds the data value and its temporal write-history (causal hash) together. This ensures that an adversary cannot forge a single block without also forging its entire causal lineage.

II-B Hypercube Arena and Multilinear Mapping

We map the arena to a Boolean hypercube of dimension dhcd_{\text{hc}}, where N=2dhcN=2^{d_{\text{hc}}}, addressing each block by a binary coordinate vector v∈{0,1}dhcv\in\{0,1\}^{d_{\text{hc}}}. The pointer chase becomes a data-dependent walk across hypercube vertices. The arena state at step tt is expressible as a multilinear polynomial Pt​(x1,…,xdhc)P_{t}(x_{1},\dots,x_{d_{\text{hc}}}) over 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2} (or an extension tower), and each step’s writes are low-degree evaluations. This imposes no overhead on the physical Prover but provides the foundation for O⁡(1)O(1) verification via binary-field folding (§II-J).

II-C Formal Definition

We formalize PoSME as a triple of algorithms (𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾,𝖵𝖾𝗋𝗂𝖿𝗒)(\mathsf{Gen},\mathsf{Prove},\mathsf{Verify}) operating over an arena AA of NN blocks.

  • •

    𝖦𝖾𝗇⁡(s,N,K)→(TK,{rt})\mathsf{Gen}(s,N,K)\to(T_{K},\{r_{t}\}). The Prover initializes AA via Init​(s,N)\textsc{Init}(s,N) and executes KK steps of Step to produce the final transcript TKT_{K} and root sequence.

  • •

    𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾⁡(TK,{rt},A,Q,R)→Π\mathsf{Prove}(T_{K},\{r_{t}\},A,Q,R)\to\Pi. The Prover commits to the root sequence and generates QQ witnesses of depth RR for Fiat-Shamir challenged steps.

  • •

    𝖵𝖾𝗋𝗂𝖿𝗒⁡(Π,s,N,K,Q,R)→{0,1}\mathsf{Verify}(\Pi,s,N,K,Q,R)\to\{0,1\}. The Verifier re-derives challenges and checks witnesses against the initial seed and committed roots.

Arena isolation. The seed ss must bind a unique task identifier (nonce, block height, challenge, etc.): s=H(task_id∥nonce)s=H(\texttt{task\_id}\|\texttt{nonce}). Because Init is deterministic, distinct seeds produce statistically independent arenas. This prevents an adversary from amortizing a single arena across multiple proof instances and is essential to the capacity-bandwidth bound analyzed in §IV-C.

Proposition 1 (Completeness).

For any seed ss and parameters (N,K,Q,R)(N,K,Q,R), an honest Prover following the protocol will always produce a proof Π\Pi such that 𝖵𝖾𝗋𝗂𝖿𝗒⁡(Π,s,N,K,Q,R)=1\mathsf{Verify}(\Pi,s,N,K,Q,R)=1.

Proof.

All algorithms are deterministic; an honest Prover computes roots and transcripts correctly, and all checks in Algorithm 4 compare honest values against themselves. ∎

II-D Proof Size and Complexity

The proof size |Π||\Pi| is dominated by the QQ witnesses. Each witness πi\pi_{i} contains openings for the challenged step and its provenance ancestors to depth RR.

Proposition 2 (Proof Size).

For a recursion depth RR, the number of blocks opened per challenge is B=∑ℓ=0R−1dℓ​(d+1)B=\sum_{\ell=0}^{R-1}d^{\ell}(d+1). The total proof size is approximately Q⋅B⋅(λ+log⁡N⋅|H|)Q\cdot B\cdot(\lambda+\log N\cdot|H|) bytes.

For the recommended parameters (N=224N{=}2^{24}, d=8d{=}8, Q=128Q{=}128), a proof at R=2R{=}2 opens B=81B{=}81 blocks (∼8.5{\sim}8.5 MB). At R=3R{=}3, B=657B{=}657 blocks (∼70{\sim}70 MB). These proofs are post-quantum secure, require no trusted setup, and are generated autonomously during execution.

II-E Proof Size Optimization

The recursion depth RR and challenge count QQ present a direct tradeoff between security margin and proof size. Table II-E provides concrete MiB-per-proof costs for implementers.

While R=3R=3 yields larger proofs, it provides exponentially higher fabrication resistance by checking the witnesses of the writers’ writers. For bandwidth-constrained environments (e.g., light clients), R=2R=2 with Q=128Q=128 offers a compact ∼\sim8 MB proof while maintaining high confidence.

II-F Arena and Initialization

The arena consists of N=2dhcN=2^{d_{\text{hc}}} blocks on a Boolean hypercube, each storing (data,causal)(\texttt{data},\texttt{causal}), each λ=256\lambda{=}256 bits, initialized deterministically from seed ss via Algorithm 1. Vertices are enumerated in standard binary order; the skip-link parent of vertex vv is v≫1v\gg 1 (right-shift by one bit), creating a binary DAG requiring Ω⁡(N)\Omega(\sqrt{N}) space to evaluate any single vertex.

II-G Step Function

Each step tt executes Algorithm 2. The coordinate vj+1v_{j+1} depends on the block at vjv_{j}; the dd reads are strictly sequential. Symbiotic binding creates bidirectional dependency: new data incorporates the old causal hash, and the new causal hash incorporates the cursor. Addressing uses binary projection: the first dhcd_{\text{hc}} bits of the hash output yield a coordinate vector v∈{0,1}dhcv\in\{0,1\}^{d_{\text{hc}}}, selecting a vertex on the Boolean hypercube.

II-H Roles of the Causal Hash

The causal hash field hh serves three distinct purposes in PoSME. We enumerate them here to prevent conflation in the security analysis that follows.

  1. 1.

    Operational binding (Construction, §II). Each block’s causal hash chains its write history into the block value, creating a per-block temporal lineage. The symbiotic bind (Algorithm 2, line 9) ensures data and causal hash are mutually dependent: neither can be computed without the other.

  2. 2.

    Soundness amplification (Theorem 1, §III). Because the causal hash is folded into the cursor at every read (Algorithm 2, line 5), any forged block produces a divergent cursor, which propagates into a divergent transcript TtT_{t}. This tightens the reduction to collision resistance: the adversary must forge both data and causal lineage simultaneously.

  3. 3.

    TMTO constant factor (Theorem 2, §III-C). When the adversary discards a block and must recompute it on a cache miss, the write chain must be traversed for both the data field and the causal field, doubling the per-miss recomputation cost (2​ρ2\rho vs. ρ\rho). This is a 2×2{\times} constant, not an asymptotic improvement.

These roles are complementary but logically independent: operational binding is a construction choice, soundness amplification is a proof-theoretic consequence, and the TMTO constant is an empirical cost multiplier.

II-I Classical Verification (Merkle/Fiat-Shamir)

PoSME supports two verification modes. The classical mode (Algorithms 3–4) uses Fiat-Shamir [22] sampled Merkle [23] witnesses and requires only a hash function; it is post-quantum secure and requires no trusted setup. The IVC mode (§II-J, Algorithms 5–6) achieves O⁡(1)O(1) proof size via binary-field folding but introduces an additional cryptographic assumption (polynomial commitment soundness).

In the classical mode, challenges are derived after the Prover commits to the complete root sequence, preventing selective disclosure.

Classical verification cost: O⁡(Q⋅dR⋅log⁡N)O(Q\cdot d^{R}\cdot\log N) hashes (∼6{\sim}6 ms desktop, 60–300 ms mobile). No arena allocation. For O⁡(1)O(1) verification, see §II-J.

II-J Constant-Size Verification via Binary-Field Folding

A fundamental limitation of legacy memory-hard functions and early PoSME verification strategies is that proof size scales with sequence length KK or requires O⁡(Q⋅dR)O(Q\cdot d^{R}) Merkle path verifications. By explicitly structuring the arena as a Boolean hypercube (§II), the construction natively integrates with recent breakthroughs in binary-field succinct arguments, notably Binius [12].

Because Binius operates over towers of binary fields and utilizes multilinear polynomial commitments, the PoSME step function maps directly to the prover’s arithmetic circuit without the heavy overhead of bit-decomposition required by prime-field SNARKs. This enables Incrementally Verifiable Computation (IVC) [25]: the Prover “folds” the proof of step tt into the proof of step t−1t{-}1. Upon completing the KK-th step, the final proof is already generated. This reduces the proof size from tens of megabytes (Table II-E) to a constant size of a few kilobytes, achieving O⁡(1)O(1) verification regardless of the number of steps KK or the recursion depth RR.

Compatibility with BLAKE3. Binius was specifically designed to efficiently verify standard bitwise operations (XOR, rotation, addition mod 2322^{32}), making it natively compatible with BLAKE3’s compression function. No change to the hash primitive is required to benefit from binary-field folding.

IVC Prove and Verify. In IVC mode, the Prover maintains a folding accumulator UtU_{t} (Algorithm 5). Each step folds the state transition into UtU_{t} via the operator ℱ\mathcal{F}. The Verifier (Algorithm 6) checks only the final accumulator, achieving O⁡(1)O(1) verification independent of KK.

IVC verification cost: O⁡(1)O(1) field operations plus a constant number of hash evaluations, independent of KK. Proof size is a few kilobytes. The classical mode (§II-I) remains available as a fallback requiring only hash function security.

II-K Concrete Arithmetization and Pipelining

To achieve the O⁡(1)O(1) verification of §II-J without violating the latency bound, the PoSME step function must be efficiently arithmetized over the binary-field tower.

BLAKE3 Boolean trace. BLAKE3 operates on 32-bit words using three operations: XOR (⊕\oplus), right rotation (⋙\ggg), and addition modulo 2322^{32} (⊞\boxplus). In a prime-field SNARK, these require bit-decomposition (∼32{\sim}32 range-check constraints per 32-bit operation). In the Binius 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2} multilinear trace, XOR is native field addition and rotation is deterministic wire-routing; both incur zero non-linear constraints. The only non-trivial arithmetization arises from the carry bits in ⊞\boxplus, represented via a low-degree carry-lookahead polynomial over 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2}. Consequently, the computational trace of the step function requires only a few thousand Boolean variables, minimizing the folding Prover’s sumcheck overhead.

Log-derivative memory checking. To verify the multilinear memory evaluations without Merkle paths in the circuit, we employ log-derivative memory checking [24] over the hypercube [12]. Each read and write at coordinate v∈{0,1}dhcv\in\{0,1\}^{d_{\text{hc}}} updates a running fractional sum in an extension field (e.g., 𝔽2128\mathbb{F}_{2^{128}}). The step circuit verifies only the O⁡(1)O(1) update to the running sum; the global memory consistency check (matching Read Set and Write Set permutation fingerprints) is deferred to the final Verifier. This replaces O⁡(log⁡N)O(\log N) Merkle constraints per access with a single finite-field addition.

Prover pipelining and fold cost. Let Tmem≈50​nsT_{\text{mem}}\approx 50\,\text{ns} be the DRAM random-access latency and TfoldT_{\text{fold}} the time to compute the Binius IVC fold for a single step. The step function requires 2​d+4=202d{+}4=20 BLAKE3 evaluations. Each BLAKE3 compression has 7 rounds ×\times 8 G-functions ×\times 4 additions mod 2322^{32} ×\times 32 carry bits =7,168=7{,}168 AND gates. With 20 compressions plus ∼1,152{\sim}1{,}152 gates for log-derivative memory checking, the total is 144,512\mathbf{144{,}512} Boolean constraints per step.

With deferred commitment (standard in IVC; the polynomial commitment is generated only for the final proof, not per-step), the per-step cost is the Binius sumcheck alone. Over ⌈log2⁡144,512⌉=18\lceil\log_{2}144{,}512\rceil=18 rounds, the sumcheck evaluates ∼2.6×106{\sim}2.6\times 10^{6} 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2} operations. Because 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2} arithmetic (XOR, AND) is SIMD-vectorizable, a single AVX-512 instruction (512 bits) processes 512 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2} operations in parallel:

Tfold=2.6×106512×1fCPU≈5,078​instr.4​GHz=1,270​ns.T_{\text{fold}}=\frac{2.6\times 10^{6}}{512}\times\frac{1}{f_{\text{CPU}}}\approx\frac{5{,}078\;\text{instr.}}{4\;\text{GHz}}=1{,}270\;\text{ns}.

The per-step DRAM cost is Tmem=(d+1)×50​ns=450​nsT_{\text{mem}}=(d{+}1)\times 50\,\text{ns}=450\,\text{ns}. Since Tfold/Tmem≈2.8T_{\text{fold}}/T_{\text{mem}}\approx 2.8, three fold threads (4 threads total on AVX-512) achieve aggregate fold throughput of 423​ns423\,\text{ns}, keeping pace with the pointer-chase. On consumer AVX2 hardware (256-bit SIMD), Tfold≈2,540​nsT_{\text{fold}}\approx 2{,}540\,\text{ns}, requiring 6 fold threads.

Critically, this parallelism is asymmetric: the adversary cannot exploit it because the pointer-chase remains strictly single-threaded, and GPUs are 14–19×{\times} slower at the sequential bottleneck (§IV). The fold parallelism benefits only the honest Prover.

III Security Analysis

III-A Threat Model

The adversary is PPT with ROM access to HH [26], receiving (s,N,K,d,Q,R)(s,N,K,d,Q,R). Goals: (1) forgery (TK′≠TKT_{K}^{\prime}\neq T_{K}), or (2) space reduction (storage <N⋅B<N\cdot B). Custom hardware permitted.

III-B Forgery Prevention

Theorem 1 (Soundness).

Any adversary producing (TK′,Croots′,π′)(T_{K}^{\prime},C_{\text{roots}}^{\prime},\pi^{\prime}) with TK′≠TKT_{K}^{\prime}\neq T_{K} that passes verification has advantage at most K⋅εcrK\cdot\varepsilon_{\text{cr}}.

Proof sketch.

Let t∗t^{*} be the first step where the adversary’s transcript diverges. Then Tt∗=H(Tt∗−1∥t∗∥cursor∥roott∗)T_{t^{*}}=H(T_{t^{*}-1}\|t^{*}\|\texttt{cursor}\|\texttt{root}_{t^{*}}) was computed with at least one differing input. Matching the honest output requires finding a collision in HH. Union bound over KK steps gives K⋅εcrK\cdot\varepsilon_{\text{cr}}. ∎

Causal hashes additionally double write-chain traversal cost (2​ρ2\rho vs ρ\rho per miss), a 2×2{\times} constant factor (see §II-H, Role 3). Their primary contribution is soundness, not TMTO amplification.

III-C TMTO Lower Bound

Write density constraint. Define the write density ρ=K/N\rho=K/N, the expected number of times each arena block is overwritten during a KK-step execution. When ρ<1\rho<1, a constant fraction of blocks are never written; the adversary can recompute them from the initialization seed at O⁡(1)O(1) cost per block, defeating the storage requirement. Meaningful TMTO resistance therefore requires:

ρ=K/N≥1(K≥N).\rho=K/N\geq 1\qquad(K\geq N). (1)

We recommend ρ≥4\rho\geq 4; see the discussion after Theorem 2.

Theorem 2 (TMTO).

An adversary storing α​N\alpha N blocks (0≤α<10\leq\alpha<1) and all KK cursors performs expected computation Tadv≥K​d​(1+(1−α)​(2​ρ+1))T_{\text{adv}}\geq Kd\bigl(1+(1{-}\alpha)(2\rho{+}1)\bigr).

Proof sketch.

Fix a step t∈[1,K]t\in[1,K]. The dd read coordinates are derived as vj=first ​dhc​ bits of ​H​(“addr”​‖c‖​j)v_{j}=\text{first }d_{\text{hc}}\text{ bits of }H(\text{``addr''}\|c\|j), where cc depends on prior reads. In the ROM, each vjv_{j} is uniform over {0,1}dhc\{0,1\}^{d_{\text{hc}}}, independent of the adversary’s stored set SS (since SS was chosen before the ROM queries). Each read hits SS with probability α\alpha and misses with probability 1−α1-\alpha.

On a miss, the adversary must reconstruct block A⁡[vj]A[v_{j}] by replaying its write chain: the block was overwritten ρ\rho times in expectation, each overwrite requiring one hash for the data field and one for the causal field, plus the final read itself, totaling 2​ρ+12\rho+1 hash evaluations per miss. (The 2×2{\times} factor from causal hashes is the constant described in §II-H, Role 3.)

Summing over KK steps of dd reads each:

Tadv≥∑t=1K∑j=0d−1[α+(1−α)​(2​ρ+1)]=K​d​(1+(1−α)​(2​ρ+1)).T_{\text{adv}}\geq\sum_{t=1}^{K}\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}\bigl[\alpha+(1{-}\alpha)(2\rho{+}1)\bigr]=Kd\bigl(1+(1{-}\alpha)(2\rho{+}1)\bigr).

The bound is tight when the adversary stores the optimal α​N\alpha N blocks (those most frequently accessed); non-uniform strategies cannot improve the expectation because ROM-uniform addressing makes all blocks equiprobable targets. ∎

Why ρ≥4\rho\geq 4. At ρ=4\rho=4 and α=0\alpha=0 (no storage), the TMTO penalty is Tadv/Thonest=1+(2⋅4+1)=10×T_{\text{adv}}/T_{\text{honest}}=1+(2\cdot 4+1)=10{\times}. This exceeds the measured ASIC advantage (∼2×{\sim}2{\times}) by 5×5{\times}: a storage-reducing adversary is strictly worse off than one with faster hardware. Verification cost is independent of ρ\rho (it depends on QQ, dd, RR, NN only), so increasing ρ\rho adds Prover wall-clock time with no Verifier penalty. The bound assumes optimal cursor storage; sparse cursors strictly increase adversary cost.

III-D Dynamic Pebbling

PoSME’s causal DAG is dynamic: edges are created during execution at ROM-uniform targets, so the graph topology is not known until the computation completes. This distinguishes it from the static graphs analyzed by Alwen et al. [5] and Boneh et al. [15], where the edge set is fixed at construction time and classical pebbling lower bounds apply directly.

The obstacle. Static-graph pebbling proofs (e.g., cumulative memory complexity bounds for Argon2 [5]) rely on two properties: (1) the graph is depth-robust, meaning no small set of nodes separates all long paths; and (2) the graph topology is known to the analyst a priori, enabling combinatorial arguments over its structure. In PoSME, neither property holds in the standard sense. The edge from step tt’s write target back to its read sources is determined by the ROM output projected onto {0,1}dhc\{0,1\}^{d_{\text{hc}}}; the analyst cannot enumerate paths without fixing the ROM, which couples the combinatorial argument to a specific oracle instantiation. Recent work by Blocki and Holman [14], extending the sustained-space framework of [27], establishes sustained-space tradeoffs for data-dependent MHFs in the parallel ROM, proving that any dynamic pebbling strategy either maintains Ω⁡(N)\Omega(N) memory for Ω⁡(N)\Omega(N) steps or incurs cumulative cost Ω⁡(N2.5−ε)\Omega(N^{2.5-\varepsilon}). Their model, which allows edges to be revealed online, directly informs our two-phase decomposition below.

Two-phase decomposition. We resolve this obstacle by decomposing PoSME’s computation graph into a static backbone (the Init DAG, whose structure is known a priori) and a dynamic overlay (the Step writes, whose edges are revealed online). The static backbone provides a deterministic termination condition for recomputation; the dynamic overlay provides an exponentially growing recursive miss penalty.

Theorem 3 (Space-Time Product).

In the ROM, any adversary storing S=α​NS=\alpha N vertices (0<α<10<\alpha<1) requires expected computation TT satisfying:

S⋅T≥α⁡(1−α)​d​W​(α,ρ)ρ⋅K2S\cdot T\;\geq\;\frac{\alpha(1{-}\alpha)\,d\,W(\alpha,\rho)}{\rho}\cdot K^{2}

where W⁡(α,ρ)=∑ℓ=0ρ[d⁡(1−α)]ℓW(\alpha,\rho)=\sum_{\ell=0}^{\rho}[d(1{-}\alpha)]^{\ell} is the expected recursive recomputation cost per cache miss. For the recommended parameters (d=8d{=}8, ρ=4\rho{=}4), S⋅T=Ω⁡(K2)S\cdot T=\Omega(K^{2}) for all constant α\alpha.

Proof sketch.

Phase 1: Static backbone (termination). The Init DAG has skip-link edges v→v≫1v\to v\gg 1, forming a binary tree of depth dhcd_{\text{hc}}. Reconstructing any Init-state vertex requires traversing its skip-link ancestry: O⁡(log⁡N)O(\log N) hash evaluations. This provides a deterministic floor for any recomputation that reaches a vertex still in its initialization state.

Phase 2: Recursive cascade (dynamic overlay). Consider a cache miss at step tt: the adversary must reconstruct vertex vjv_{j}, which was last written at step t′<tt^{\prime}<t. That write read dd vertices, each missing independently with probability (1−α)(1{-}\alpha) in the ROM (by the same uniformity argument as Theorem 2). Each secondary miss triggers further recomputation, forming a Galton-Watson branching process with expected offspring d⁡(1−α)d(1{-}\alpha).

Depth bound. Under ROM-uniform writes (one write per step to a uniform random vertex), the time since the last write to any given vertex is geometric with success probability 1/N1/N, giving expected gap NN and standard deviation N⁡(N−1)≈N\sqrt{N(N{-}1)}\approx N. Each recursion level regresses the timeline by one such gap (∼N{\sim}N steps). After ρ=K/N\rho=K/N levels, the cumulative regression covers ∼ρ​N=K{\sim}\rho N=K steps, reaching the Init state, where Phase 1 terminates the branch at O⁡(log⁡N)O(\log N) cost. The expected number of live misses at depth ℓ\ell is [d⁡(1−α)]ℓ[d(1{-}\alpha)]^{\ell}, giving total expected work per primary miss:

W⁡(α,ρ)=∑ℓ=0ρ[d⁡(1−α)]ℓ.W(\alpha,\rho)=\sum_{\ell=0}^{\rho}[d(1{-}\alpha)]^{\ell}.

When d⁡(1−α)>1d(1{-}\alpha)>1 (i.e., α<1−1/d\alpha<1{-}1/d), WW grows exponentially in ρ\rho.

Product. Each of the KK steps performs dd reads, each missing with probability (1−α)(1{-}\alpha) and costing WW expected hash evaluations. Total: T≥K​d​(1−α)​WT\geq Kd(1{-}\alpha)W. Multiplying by S=α​NS=\alpha N and substituting K=ρ​NK=\rho N:

S⋅T≥α⁡(1−α)​d​W​(α,ρ)ρ⋅K2.S\cdot T\;\geq\;\frac{\alpha(1{-}\alpha)\,d\,W(\alpha,\rho)}{\rho}\cdot K^{2}.

∎

Concrete evaluation (d=8d{=}8, ρ=4\rho{=}4). Table III shows the space-time product at representative storage fractions. The critical threshold is αc=1−1/d=7/8\alpha_{c}=1-1/d=7/8: below this, the branching process is supercritical and WW grows exponentially. Even at αc\alpha_{c} the bound exceeds K2K^{2}.

At the adversary-optimal storage α∗=1/(ρ+2)=1/6\alpha^{*}=1/(\rho{+}2)=1/6, the space-time product is 645​K2645\,K^{2}, over 300×300{\times} the honest cost of 2​K22\,K^{2}. Even storing 7/87/8 of the arena (a mere 12.5% reduction) yields S⋅T≥1.09​K2S\cdot T\geq 1.09\,K^{2}. Any meaningful storage reduction triggers exponential recomputation.

Strengthened bound: temporal staleness. Theorem 3 conservatively assumes the adversary’s cache hit rate is α\alpha at every recursion depth. This overstates the adversary’s capability. The adversary stores current vertex states (at execution step tt), but reconstruction requires historical states (at step t′<tt^{\prime}<t). Under ROM-uniform writes, vertex uu is rewritten in the interval (t′,t](t^{\prime},t] with probability 1−e−(t−t′)/N1-e^{-(t-t^{\prime})/N}, rendering the stored value stale. Since each recursion level regresses ∼N{\sim}N steps, the effective hit rate at depth ℓ\ell decays exponentially.

Theorem 4 (Temporal Staleness).

Under the conditions of Theorem 3, the effective cache hit rate at recursion depth ℓ\ell is at most α​e−ℓ\alpha e^{-\ell}, and the expected recomputation cost per miss satisfies:

W∗​(α,ρ)≥∑ℓ=0ρ∏k=0ℓ−1d⁡(1−α​e−k).W^{*}\!(\alpha,\rho)\;\geq\;\sum_{\ell=0}^{\rho}\;\prod_{k=0}^{\ell-1}d\bigl(1-\alpha e^{-k}\bigr).

For the recommended parameters (d=8d{=}8, ρ=4\rho{=}4), the branching factor d⁡(1−α​e−k)>1d(1-\alpha e^{-k})>1 for all k≥1k\geq 1 and all α<1\alpha<1.

Proof sketch.

The adversary maintains α​N\alpha N current vertex states. At recursion depth ℓ\ell, reconstruction needs vertex uu’s state from ∼ℓ​N{\sim}\ell N steps in the past. Under ROM-uniform writes (one write per step to a uniform random vertex), the probability that uu was not rewritten in ℓ​N\ell N steps is (1−1/N)ℓ​N≈e−ℓ(1-1/N)^{\ell N}\approx e^{-\ell}. The stored state is valid only if uu was not rewritten, so the effective hit rate is α​e−ℓ\alpha e^{-\ell}.

The expected offspring at depth ℓ\ell is d⁡(1−α​e−ℓ)d(1-\alpha e^{-\ell}). For d=8d=8 and ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1: d⁡(1−α​e−1)=8​(1−α/e)>1d(1-\alpha e^{-1})=8(1-\alpha/e)>1 for all α<e⁡(1−1/8)=2.38\alpha<e(1{-}1/8)=2.38, which holds for any α∈[0,1)\alpha\in[0,1). Thus the branching process is supercritical at every depth beyond the first level, regardless of α\alpha. ∎

Elimination of the critical threshold. Under Theorem 3, the critical storage fraction αc=1−1/d=7/8\alpha_{c}=1{-}1/d=7/8 separates the supercritical and subcritical regimes. Temporal staleness eliminates this threshold entirely: even at α=7/8\alpha=7/8, the level-1 branching factor is d⁡(1−α/e)=5.42d(1{-}\alpha/e)=5.42, driving the recomputation cost from W=5W=5 to W∗=338W^{*}=338. Table IV compares both bounds.

The gain concentrates where it matters most: near the old critical threshold. An adversary storing 95% of the arena now faces S⋅T≥12​K2S\cdot T\geq 12\,K^{2}, a 6×6{\times} penalty over honest computation, versus the basic bound’s marginal 0.16​K20.16\,K^{2}.

Extension to adaptive strategies. Theorems 3 and 4 assume the adversary fixes a storage set before execution. We now show that adaptive caching provides no advantage under the ROM.

Theorem 5 (Adaptive Bound).

At each step tt, the adaptive adversary’s storage set StS_{t} is a function of {T0,…,Tt−1}\{T_{0},\ldots,T_{t-1}\} and prior ROM queries. All dd read addresses {v0,…,vd−1}\{v_{0},\ldots,v_{d-1}\} satisfy Pr[vj∈St]=α\Pr[v_{j}\in S_{t}]=\alpha for every j∈[0,d−1]j\in[0,d{-}1]. The adaptive adversary’s miss rate is identical to the static case.

Proof sketch.

The address v0v_{0} is computable from Tt−1T_{t-1} via a single ROM query: the adversary knows which vertex to read, but reading it requires v0∈Stv_{0}\in S_{t}. Since |St|=α​N|S_{t}|=\alpha N and v0v_{0} is a ROM output uniform over {0,1}dhc\{0,1\}^{d_{\text{hc}}}, Pr[v0∈St]=α\Pr[v_{0}\in S_{t}]=\alpha, no better than any other read.

For j≥1j\geq 1: the cursor cj=H(cj−1∥A[vj−1].d∥A[vj−1].h)c_{j}=H(c_{j-1}\|A[v_{j-1}].d\|A[v_{j-1}].h) depends on A⁡[vj−1]A[v_{j-1}], which is revealed only after the (j−1)(j{-}1)-th read completes. The address vj=H⁡(“addr”​‖cj‖​j)v_{j}=H(\text{``addr''}\|c_{j}\|j) is therefore a ROM query whose output is independent of StS_{t} (fixed before this query). Thus Pr[vj∈St]=α\Pr[v_{j}\in S_{t}]=\alpha for all jj.

Lookahead. Predicting read addresses for step t+1t{+}1 requires computing TtT_{t}, which requires executing step tt, which is the sequential work being bounded. The adversary has at most one-step lookahead, and that step’s addresses are already conditioned on values the adversary may not possess. ∎

Theorem 5 shows that the static-storage bounds of Theorems 3 and 4 apply without modification to adaptive adversaries. No factor loss is incurred.

III-E Vertex Coverage and Mixing

The TMTO analysis (Theorems 2–5) assumes ROM-uniform vertex access. We now validate this assumption both mathematically and empirically.

Theorem 6 (Vertex Coverage).

In the ROM with parameters NN, KK, dd, ρ=K/N\rho=K/N:

  1. (a)

    The write count WvW_{v} for each vertex vv converges to Poisson⁡(ρ)\mathrm{Poisson}(\rho) as N→∞N\to\infty. The read count RvR_{v} converges to Poisson⁡(d​ρ)\mathrm{Poisson}(d\rho).

  2. (b)

    The maximum read count satisfies maxv⁡Rv<(1+δ)​d​ρ\max_{v}R_{v}<(1{+}\delta)\,d\rho with probability ≥1−N⋅e−δ2dρ/3\geq 1-N\cdot e^{-\delta^{2}d\rho/3} for 0<δ<10<\delta<1.

  3. (c)

    Successive read addresses vj,vj+1v_{j},v_{j+1} within a step are pairwise independent in the ROM (distinct oracle queries with distinct inputs).

Proof sketch.

(a) Write addresses are ROM-uniform over NN vertices, one per step. The classical balls-in-bins Poisson limit gives Wv→Poisson⁡(ρ)W_{v}\to\mathrm{Poisson}(\rho). Read addresses are similarly uniform; dd per step gives Rv→Poisson⁡(d​ρ)R_{v}\to\mathrm{Poisson}(d\rho).

(b) By the multiplicative Chernoff bound, Pr[Rv>(1+δ)μ]≤e−δ2μ/3\Pr[R_{v}>(1{+}\delta)\mu]\leq e^{-\delta^{2}\mu/3} where μ=d​ρ\mu=d\rho. Union bounding over NN vertices, Pr[maxvRv>(1+δ)μ]≤Ne−δ2μ/3\Pr[\max_{v}R_{v}>(1{+}\delta)\mu]\leq Ne^{-\delta^{2}\mu/3}. For d=8d{=}8, ρ=4\rho{=}4 (μ=32\mu{=}32), N=224N{=}2^{24}, δ=1\delta{=}1: 224⋅e−32/3≈3.7×10−6⋅224≈622^{24}\cdot e^{-32/3}\approx 3.7\times 10^{-6}\cdot 2^{24}\approx 62. The probability that any vertex exceeds 2​μ=642\mu=64 reads is <62/N<62/N; no vertex exceeds 3​μ3\mu with probability >1−2−40>1-2^{-40}.

(c) vj+1=first ​dhc​ bits of ​H​(“addr”​‖cj+1‖​(j+1))v_{j+1}=\text{first }d_{\text{hc}}\text{ bits of }H(\text{``addr''}\|c_{j+1}\|(j{+}1)) where cj+1=H(cj∥A[vj].d∥A[vj].h)c_{j+1}=H(c_{j}\|A[v_{j}].d\|A[v_{j}].h). This is a distinct ROM query from vjv_{j}’s (different cursor input), so the outputs are independent. ∎

Empirical validation. We executed the full PoSME address generation chain with BLAKE3 at the recommended production parameters: N=224N{=}2^{24} (1 GiB arena), ρ=4\rho{=}4, d=8d{=}8, K=67,108,864K{=}67{,}108{,}864 steps, 536,870,912536{,}870{,}912 total reads. The Rust implementation completed in 244 s (3,637 ns/step), confirming latency-bound behavior. Table V summarizes the results.

The chi-squared statistics are indistinguishable from perfect uniformity to four decimal places. The observed standard deviations match Poisson predictions (d​ρ\sqrt{d\rho} and ρ\sqrt{\rho}) to four significant figures across all 2242^{24} vertices. The unwritten fraction matches the theoretical e−ρe^{-\rho} to 0.12%0.12\% relative error. These results confirm that BLAKE3’s address generation is empirically indistinguishable from the ROM at the recommended production parameters.

III-F ASIC Resistance

PoSME is designed to be latency-dominated: hash computation is a structural minority of per-step cost (<3%<3\% at 1 GiB arena). The bottleneck is DRAM random-access latency. Fig. 2 shows the cost breakdown across six memory technologies. Hash cost (3 ns) is constant; memory latency varies by type but dominates in all cases. GDDR6 has the lowest CAS latency (∼8{\sim}8 ns) but GPU cores are 14–19×\times slower at sequential pointer-chasing (Table VII), negating the memory advantage entirely.

Real random-access latency (tRCD + CL + controller overhead) raises the floor from ∼10{\sim}10 ns to 40–50 ns on any hardware. The measured HBM3-vs-DDR5 advantage is only 1.3×1.3{\times}. DRAM latency has improved 1.3×1.3{\times} over two decades while bandwidth improved 20×20{\times} [7], making PoSME’s latency bound structurally more durable than bandwidth-based resistance [3, 4].

IV Empirical Validation

IV-A Experimental Protocol

We benchmarked PoSME on 17 platforms spanning ARM64 and x86 architectures, ranging from 1–32 vCPUs, utilizing both DDR4 and DDR5 memory. Our evaluation also included cloud-based GPU instances (NVIDIA T4, A10G, L4, A100, and H100) to measure the advantage of massively parallel hardware. The reference implementation was written in Rust with BLAKE3 as the underlying hash function. All tests were performed on a 1 GiB arena (N=224N=2^{24}) to ensure the working set exceeded the L3 cache of all tested processors.

IV-B Performance Results

Hash Fraction. Across all 17 CPU platforms, the hash computation fraction remained between 1.4% and 3.1% (Table VI). The CPU spends over 96% of step time waiting for DRAM random access.

Prover Wall-Clock Time. For the recommended production parameters (N=224N=2^{24} (1 GiB), K=4​N=67×106K=4N=67\times 10^{6} steps), the total Prover wall-clock time is approximately 120–200 seconds (2–3.3 minutes) on modern hardware, consistent with the observed 1783–3000 ns per step. Step times varied 2.3×\times (1783–4047 ns), but the hash fraction remained in a tight band because both hash and memory scale together on any given machine. Step cost increases with arena size as the working set exceeds L3 cache, confirming memory-bound behavior.

GPU Performance Gap. To directly measure the adversary’s hardware advantage, we ran the PoSME pointer-chase loop as a CUDA kernel on GPU cores accessing GPU memory (HBM/GDDR), comparing against the host CPU running the identical algorithm on system DRAM. The results (Table VII): GPUs are 14–19×\times slower than the host CPU.

GPU cores are optimized for parallel throughput, not sequential pointer-chasing. A single CUDA thread at ∼1.5{\sim}1.5 GHz cannot compete with a CPU core at ∼3.5{\sim}3.5 GHz for sequential dependent loads. The GPU’s memory bandwidth advantage is irrelevant because the pointer-chase is latency-bound, not bandwidth-bound.

The ASIC advantage (1.3×\times measured for HBM3 vs DDR5 random access) requires a custom sequential core paired with HBM, hardware that does not exist commercially. All purchasable accelerators (GPUs) are strictly worse than consumer CPUs.

IV-C Throughput and the Capacity-Bandwidth Bound

The preceding analysis addresses per-instance latency. A sophisticated adversary may instead target throughput: running many independent PoSME instances in parallel to amortize the per-instance GPU penalty. GPUs hide sequential latency behind massive memory bandwidth (e.g., 3 TB/s on the H100). However, arena isolation (§II) forces each instance to allocate a unique MM-byte arena, converting the attack from a bandwidth problem into a capacity problem.

Capacity choke. An NVIDIA H100 [32] has 80 GiB of HBM3 VRAM. With a 1 GiB arena per instance, the GPU accommodates at most 80 concurrent executions. At the physical HBM3 random-access floor of ∼20{\sim}20 ns per 64-byte read, each instance consumes 64​B/20​ns=3.264\,\text{B}/20\,\text{ns}=3.2 GB/s. The 80 instances collectively use ∼256{\sim}256 GB/s, less than 9% of the H100’s 3 TB/s bandwidth. The GPU is memory-capacity-bound, not bandwidth-bound.

Economic comparison. At comparable capital outlay, commodity DDR5 platforms provide 1010–20×20{\times} more aggregate arena capacity per dollar than HBM3-equipped accelerators, with the exact ratio depending on market conditions. The disparity grows with arena size: a 4 GiB arena reduces an 80 GiB GPU to 20 instances while a 16 GiB desktop still runs 3.

Table VIII summarizes the capacity-bandwidth mismatch across GPU architectures.

As GPU bandwidth scales faster than capacity (a structural trend in HBM design [7]), the capacity-bandwidth mismatch worsens for the adversary. PoSME’s 1 GiB arena is specifically sized to exploit this gap.

V Parameters

Initialization. Arena initialization (skip-link DAG over NN blocks) requires ∼4{\sim}4 s for 1 GiB (measured). This is a one-time cost per seed, amortized over the KK-step computation.

Recursion depth. At R=2R{=}2, the Verifier opens a challenged step’s dd reads and each read’s writer, but not the writers’ reads. An adversary can fabricate a block bb by choosing an arbitrary writer step ww with a plausible cursor, since ww’s own reads are never checked. At R=3R{=}3, the Verifier also opens ww’s dd reads and their writers, forcing the adversary to produce d3=512d^{3}{=}512 mutually consistent causal hashes. The cost of fabrication grows as dRd^{R}; higher RR provides exponentially stronger soundness but linearly larger proofs.

VI From Sequential Work to Verifiable Time

A common misconception is that a proof of sequential work equivalently proves wall-clock time. While PoSME enforces a lower bound on the number of sequential steps Ω⁡(K)\Omega(K), an adversary with specialized hardware can execute these steps faster than a commodity processor.

VI-A The Economic Bound

Our benchmarks show a ∼1.3×{\sim}1.3{\times} potential speedup for custom sequential-core ASICs with HBM3 memory. However, the cost-to-performance ratio for such hardware is extremely prohibitive. Building a custom silicon tape-out simply to gain a 30% lead over a $500 consumer laptop is economically irrational for most attack scenarios. PoSME thus provides an economic bound on acceleration that is structurally tighter than bandwidth-bound functions like Argon2id (88–16×16{\times}).

VI-B Bridging the Gap to VDFs

To transform PoSME into a true Verifiable Delay Function (VDF) or a high-precision time-binding primitive, we suggest three architectural wrappers:

  1. 1.

    VDF-PoSME Hybrid: The final transcript TKT_{K} can be used as the input to a sequential VDF (e.g., Wesolowski [11], Pietrzak [19]). The PoSME component ensures the computation was memory-hard and ASIC-resistant, while the VDF provides a mathematical guarantee of the time elapsed.

  2. 2.

    Hardware Attestation (TEE): If the Prover executes within a Trusted Execution Environment, the TEE can provide signed hardware timestamps for T0T_{0} and TKT_{K}. This binds the cryptographic work to a physical, trusted clock.

  3. 3.

    Randomness Beacons: Provers can be forced to periodically absorb unpredictable external data (e.g., Bitcoin block hashes) into the cursor cc. This proves the computation could not have completed before the beacon was released, pinning execution to real-world events.

VII Limitations

Steps, not time. PoSME proves sequential memory execution, not elapsed wall-clock time. A custom sequential-core ASIC with HBM3 could gain ∼1.3×{\sim}1.3{\times}; such hardware does not exist commercially. Bridging the gap to verifiable time requires an external wrapper (§VI).

ROM dependence. The security analysis (Theorems 1–5) assumes the Random Oracle Model. Theorem 6 validates the assumption empirically for BLAKE3 at the recommended parameters (χ2/df=1.0004\chi^{2}/\text{df}=1.0004 at N=224N{=}2^{24}), but proving the space-time bound in the standard model (e.g., under collision resistance alone) remains open, as it does for all memory-hard functions in current use [5].

IVC implementation. The O⁡(1)O(1) verification design (§II-J, §II-K) is validated analytically (1,270​ns1{,}270\,\text{ns} fold, 144,512 constraints) but not by a production Binius implementation. Three fold threads keep pace with the pointer-chase on AVX-512 hardware.

Side channels. Data-dependent addressing leaks access patterns via cache timing on shared hardware. Because PoSME operates on public state derived from a public seed, the access pattern is public knowledge and provides no shortcut to forgery. The channel is informational, not exploitable.

Reproducibility. A reference benchmark with pre-compiled binaries and CUDA source is provided as ancillary material in the repository’s anc/ directory. All code is licensed under Apache-2.0.

VIII Conclusion

PoSME fills a gap between VDFs, PoSW, MHFs, and PoST by combining mutable arena state, data-dependent pointer chasing, and symbiotic causal binding into a single latency-bound primitive. The construction requires no trusted setup and achieves three properties that no prior primitive provides simultaneously: Ω⁡(K)\Omega(K) sequential memory-step enforcement, 10×10{\times} TMTO resistance at ρ=4\rho{=}4, and a ∼2×{\sim}2{\times} ASIC bound determined by DRAM physics rather than ALU speed.

The security analysis resolves the principal open question for dynamic causal DAGs: a formal S⋅T=Ω⁡(K2)S\cdot T=\Omega(K^{2}) lower bound (Theorem 3), strengthened by temporal cache staleness (Theorem 4) and extended to adaptive adversaries with no factor loss (Theorem 5). Empirical validation at the full recommended scale (N=224N{=}2^{24}, 5.4×1085.4{\times}10^{8} reads) confirms ROM uniformity to four significant figures (Theorem 6).

Benchmarks across 17 CPU and 4 GPU platforms validate the core claim: no commercially available hardware, including NVIDIA’s H100, outperforms a consumer laptop at PoSME. GPU throughput is choked by VRAM capacity, giving commodity CPUs a 1010–20×20{\times} aggregate advantage per dollar.

The binary-field algebraic structure is additionally compatible with emerging Processing-in-Memory architectures [30], where the latency bound would tighten from ∼50{\sim}50 ns (wire travel) to ∼10{\sim}10 ns (sense amplifier limit).
